newsitem.title: USA: Classic art to shed new light on glitzy Vegas.
newsitem.headline: Classic art to shed new light on glitzy Vegas.

text.p: In a town that lures millions of visitors with fast money and topless showgirls, the latest tourist attraction coming to Las Vegas is, for a change, art.

Mirage Resorts Inc. is a year away from opening the most expensive hotel casino here, the $1.5 billion Bellagio. But already Chairman Steve Wynn is raising customer expectations -- and investor eyebrows -- with plans to include $100 million of paintings by artists such as Claude Monet and Pablo Picasso.
"I phrase the budget as $1.4 billion plus art," Chief Financial Officer Dan Lee said in a recent interview.

Lee said he describes the hotel's price that way because he doesn't want stockholders and others to think construction costs are off track. In fact, he said, Bellagio is on budget and on schedule for an opening on Sept. 3, 1998.
But the cost of art, which was always been pegged as one of the resorts' drawing cards, has risen from $50 million to $100 million.
"I have heard some groans and moans from shareholders," Bear Stearns analyst Jason Ader said, "But at the end of the day, I think shareholders have confidence in Steve Wynn."

In Las Vegas, Wynn's success has been nothing short of phenomenal, first with the Golden Nugget downtown and later with The Mirage, which opened in 1989, and Treasure Island on the city's famed "Strip."
In 1989, opening the Mirage was a huge risk for the company because it was deep in debt and operated only two small hotels.
Some investors have voiced concern about Mirage's debt this time, too, because the company will borrow about $1.6 billion to finish Bellagio and a sister hotel in Mississippi.
Beyond using the artwork to entice high-rolling customers, Bellagio promises to be the most luxurious hotel in Las Vegas.

Its design, replicating an Italian village, includes a man-made lake with over a thousand fountains. Each will shoot water as high as 150 feet in the air during a "ballet" of synchronized lights and music.
Bellagio will feature upscale restaurants, two of which will be run by the owners New York's famed Le Cirque and housed in Mediterranean-style villas on the lake.
Retail shops will include high fashion names such as Gucci, Chanel, Hermes and Tiffany.
Bellagio's top-line suites will be mansion-sized and its standard guest rooms will be 15 percent to 20 percent larger than most other luxury hotels.
